title: Half treble in depth
subtitle: UK htr — the compromise stitch with three loops at the top
excerpt: The half treble sits between the double crochet and the treble in height and texture. Its three loops at the top produce a slightly different fabric character from any other basic stitch — and those three loops are the base of the puff stitch.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776). Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 2. Half treble as a garment and edging stitch.
heroPrompt: A swatch of half treble crochet in DK cotton, showing the distinctive three-loop top of each stitch, cream yarn on natural linen background.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stitch one step taller than double crochet and one step shorter than treble. Worked by yarning over before inserting the hook, then pulling through all three resulting loops at once. Equals US half double crochet (hdc).

The extra loop that sits at the back of a half treble, visible as a horizontal bar. Working into this third loop instead of the top V leaves the V loops visible on the front face, creating a ribbed or knit-look texture.

content.text: The
half treble

is different from every other basic stitch in one respect: it ends with three loops on the hook rather than two, and pulls them all off at once. That single characteristic gives the stitch its character. The fabric is slightly softer, slightly less structured than treble, and slightly taller and looser than double crochet.
Working a half treble
Yarn over before inserting the hook (wrap once, before the stitch).
Insert the hook through the next stitch, under both top loops.
Yarn over again and pull a loop back through the stitch. Three loops on the hook.
Yarn over one final time and pull through all three loops at once. One loop remains.

Look at the top of the finished stitch. There is a V on the surface (the top two loops) and a third loop sitting just behind it, slightly lower. That third loop is the distinctive half treble feature — it is the
third loop
Working into the third loop

Working into the third loop only (the horizontal bar at the back of the stitch) instead of the top V leaves those front loops visible on the right side of the fabric. The effect is a knit-look or ribbed texture that reads completely differently from standard half treble fabric. This technique is used for waistcoat stitch (also called the knit stitch in crochet) and any pattern that calls for a faux-rib with half trebles.
Work the foundation row in standard half treble.
On the next row, after the turning chain, tilt the work slightly toward you so you can see the horizontal third loop behind each stitch.
Insert the hook under that third loop only (the horizontal bar), not into the top V.
Complete the half treble normally. The unworked V-loops sit forward on the face.
Working a swatch
Foundation chain: 15 ch. Turn.
Row 1: ch 2 (counts as first htr in this swatch), htr in 3rd chain from hook and in each chain across (15 htr including turning chain). Turn.
Row 2: ch 2 (counts as first htr), skip the first stitch at base of turning chain, htr in each stitch across, last htr into top of turning chain (15 htr). Turn.
Repeat row 2 for 8 rows. Fasten off.
Common mistakes

attrs.heading: Half treble problems
attrs.intro: Four issues that come up with half trebles.

items.symptom: Three loops turn into two before the final yarn over
items.cause: The initial yarn over before inserting the hook slipped off during the insertion.
items.fix: Hold the yarn over snugly against the hook shaft while inserting. A slight clockwise roll of the hook as you insert helps keep the loop in place.

items.symptom: The turning chain-2 leaves a noticeable hole at the start of the row
items.cause: The turning chain is too tall for the stitch height, leaving a gap between the chain and the first actual stitch.
items.fix: Some makers prefer a chain-1 turning chain (not counted) for half treble rows, which closes the gap. Try both and see which matches your tension.

items.symptom: Cannot find the third loop to work into
items.cause: Looking at the wrong part of the stitch — the third loop hides just behind and below the top V.
items.fix: Hold the work at a slight angle so the stitch faces away from you. The horizontal third loop appears as a bar behind the top V.

items.symptom: Stitch count drops on the final row
items.cause: Missing the last htr into the top of the turning chain.
items.fix: The top of the turning chain is the chain-2 at the start of the previous row. It has a V-loop at its tip; work the final htr into that V.

content.text: What to try next

The puff stitch is the natural next step: it uses the same initial yarn over as the half treble, repeated five or six times into the same stitch before drawing all the loops off at once. The third-loop half treble leads directly into the waistcoat stitch and into Tunisian simple stitch, which uses a similar insert-and-hold mechanism.
